name: Vertical stripes / monochrome elongation
lead: Vertical stripes and single-colour outfits are a common piece of style advice, based on the belief that they make a person look taller and slimmer, while horizontal stripes make them look shorter and wider.[3] Researchers have examined the underlying visual illusion, and the results are mixed.

A 2011 study in i-Perception reported that a square of horizontal lines looked taller and narrower than the same square drawn with vertical lines, and titled its finding as horizontal stripes not making people look fatter.[1] A 2013 follow-up reported a similar result for filled squares and found the effect varied between observers.[2]
infobox: Vertical stripes elongate; horizontal stripes widen[3]

paras: A 2022 study of an 1813 Japanese beauty handbook found the belief that striped clothing alters perceived body shape was already established over 200 years ago, when vertical striped patterns were popularised.[3] Monochrome dressing is described by proponents as creating one uninterrupted line.

The vertical-horizontal illusion makes a vertical line look longer than a horizontal line of equal length, and the effect persists even when viewers know the lines are equal.[4] The Helmholtz illusion concerns filled versus unfilled space.[1]

The 2011 study applied this to fashion and reported that horizontal stripes made squares look taller and narrower, contradicting the common belief.[1] A 2013 paper reported the same direction but found it appeared mainly in people who were already fit and not for everyone.[2] These studies used abstract squares and (in part) clothed figures; the PubMed pages only gave abstract snippets, and no study specifically on monochrome outfits was found.
No clinical studies found. Perception experiments on stripe orientation exist, summarised above.[1][2]

timeline.event: A Japanese beauty handbook records the belief that stripe direction affects perceived body shape.[3]
Thompson and Mikellidou publish a Helmholtz illusion study applied to fashion.[1]
Ashida and colleagues publish a follow-up on who the effect applies to.[2]

card.summary: Dressing in vertical stripes or one colour to look taller and slimmer; the small perception literature points the other way for stripes.
card.note: Published stripe studies report horizontal stripes looking narrower, contrary to the common belief.

quick.overview:
The popular belief is that vertical stripes and head-to-toe single colours make a person look taller and slimmer.

Researchers have tested stripe direction in perception experiments. Two i-Perception studies reported horizontal stripes looking thinner, though the effect varied between viewers. No study on monochrome outfits was found.
quick.mechanism: The idea rests on optical illusions such as the vertical-horizontal and Helmholtz illusions, where line direction and filled space alter perceived length and width.
